summary: Audited 4 tier-2 pages (ranks 43-46) with full OUTPUT CONTRACT blocks; verified 3-6 factual claims per page against EPA, ConEd, and authoritative sources; identified fee-cluster overlap and instant-exit patterns; mapped seasonal-water cluster vs restructured siblings.
findings: PAGE: why-is-my-water-bill-higher-in-winter — RATING: C — Serviceable but thin (846 words) for an 8-cause list that implies depth. INTENT: diagnose winter bill spike — ALIGNED. ISSUES: each cause gets 1-2 sentences; lacks the practical how-to the slug promises; sections 'Longer billing cycle', 'Indoor leaks', 'More hot water' are each ~50 words — barely outlines; no worked example of comparing billing days; 'Estimated reads' section mentions the correction spike but doesn't explain how to spot it on a bill; FAQ section (5 questions) is generic boilerplate — no decision rules. FACTS: 'EPA WaterSense advises reviewing winter use for leaks' — CONFIRMED (epa.gov/watersense/fix-leak-week, retrieved 2026-08-29); 'Family of four >12,000 gal/month likely serious leak' — CONFIRMED (same source); 'Average household leaks waste 9,400 gal/yr' — CONFIRMED (epa.gov/watersense/statistics-and-facts, retrieved 2026-08-29). WEAKCOPY: 'Winter water bills rise most often because of a longer billing cycle, hidden indoor leaks, more hot water use, or a sewer averaging change.' — vague, no decision criteria to distinguish among 4 causes. FIXES: (1) Expand each cause with a concrete example — e.g., 'Compare the billing period days: a 35-day vs 28-day cycle is 25% more water on paper'; (2) Add a diagnostic decision tree step: 'If usage per day is flat but total is up → check billing days. If usage per day is up → check toilet dye test first.'; (3) Remove generic FAQs and replace with actionable ones (e.g., 'My winter bill is $50 higher than last winter — what do I open first?'); (4) Link to '06-water-bill-too-high' for the ranked-cause method instead of repeating shallow content. EFFORT: M · IMPACT: H — page is thin, fixing makes it authoritative. SEO: 'why is my water bill higher in winter' is good keyword-target; add schema to each FAQ; add 'seasonal water use' to tags.

PAGE: 20-utility-bill-proration-explained — RATING: D — Very thin (484 words) and misaligned. INTENT: explain partial-period (prorated) billing — PARTIAL. The page is a procedural checklist for how to 'review' a partial bill, but the slug promises 'proration explained' — there is no definition of proration, no calculation example, no explanation of daily-rate × days formula. ISSUES: Title says 'How to Review a Partial-Period Utility Bill' but the page lacks any actual review methodology; no worked example recomputing (daily rate × days) — user cannot verify their own bill; the ConEd sources are generic utility billing pages that don't specifically address partial-period calculation; the 'Questions for the Provider' section is generic and doesn't tell the user what answer to expect; zero mention of the standard proration formula (fixed charges ÷ days in billing cycle × days of service). FACTS: 'Con Edison sample bill identifies service dates' — CONFIRMED (coned.com page exists, retrieved 2026-08-29); 'Con Edison explains account holders can submit meter readings' — CONFIRMED (same source, mentions submitting meter reading to avoid estimated bill); the page claims providers 'may not prorate fixed charges by day' — UNVERIFIED (no specific tariff cited, varies by jurisdiction). WEAKCOPY: 'Do not assume every provider prorates fixed charges by day, uses the same move-in/out rule, treats real-estate closings alike' — hedging without providing the actual rules. FIXES: (1) Rewrite the page to define proration: 'Proration = (daily rate) × (days of service)'; (2) Add a worked example: 'Your fixed charge is $20/month ÷ 30 days × 15 days of service = $10'; (3) Add a section on what to expect from different utilities (water vs electric vs gas proration differs); (4) Remove 'Questions for the Provider' and replace with a self-diagnosis checklist; (5) Note that the ConEd page is about meter-reading, not proration — replace or supplement with a specific proration tariff example from a known utility; (6) Add internal link to 'understanding your bill' pages. EFFORT: M · IMPACT: H — current page fails the slug's promise. SEO: 'prorated utility bill' keyword opportunity unmet; add 'partial month billing' and 'move-in move-out bill' to keywords.

PAGE: why-is-my-water-bill-higher-in-summer — RATING: B — Solid but has structural issues. INTENT: diagnose summer bill spike — ALIGNED. Good word count (1,280), clear sections, and cites the key EPA numbers. ISSUES: (1) The '7 common reasons' section is a list without diagnostic priority — a user with a toilet leak will read through all 7 before the page tells them to check the toilet first; (2) 'How tiered pricing can make the increase feel bigger' is duplicated content — this page and tiered-water-rates-explained both cover the same mechanism almost verbatim; (3) The 'Summer Water Usage Breakdown' table (50-200 gal/day for lawn) has no source citation — this is an invented claim; (4) 'The first three things to check' section is good but the link to 'water service charge explained' is tangential to a spike diagnosis; (5) The page does not reference EPA's 12,000-gal winter benchmark even though it's useful context for seasonal comparison. FACTS: 'Outdoor water accounts for >30% of household use, up to 60% in arid regions' — CONFIRMED (epa.gov/watersense/statistics-and-facts, retrieved 2026-08-29); 'Up to 50% of outdoor water lost to wind, evaporation, runoff' — CONFIRMED (same source); 'Tiered pricing charges more per unit once usage passes certain thresholds' — CONFIRMED (standard utility practice, verified via multiple utility rate cards); 'A small continuous leak can add up over a 30-day period' — CONFIRMED (EPA: average leak wastes 9,400 gal/yr); Summer usage table (50-200 gal/day lawn) — NEEDS HUMAN REVIEW — no source cited, plausible but unsupported. WEAKCOPY: 'Summer water bills have a pattern: they look normal, then the heat arrives, and the next statement is noticeably higher.' — filler, no diagnostic value. FIXES: (1) Reorder the 7 causes by likelihood — toilet leak #1, irrigation #2, tiered pricing #3; (2) Remove the tiered-pricing section or keep only a 2-sentence summary with a link to tiered-water-rates-explained (avoid duplication); (3) Source the summer usage table or remove it; (4) Add a cross-reference to 'why is my water bill higher in winter' for seasonal comparison; (5) Add the EPA winter benchmark as a way to identify serious leaks. EFFORT: M · IMPACT: M — page works but has duplication and unsourced data. SEO: 'summer water bill higher' keyword; add 'seasonal water usage' to tags.

PAGE: tiered-water-rates-explained — RATING: B— (B-minus). INTENT: explain tiered water rate structures — ALIGNED. Good word count (3,092), comprehensive, with worked calculations. ISSUES: (1) The Colorado HB 1090 claim ('January 1, 2026, HB 1090 in Colorado requires that tenants cannot be charged more than the actual amount billed') — NEEDS HUMAN REVIEW — my search did not confirm this exact 2026 date or scope; (2) The CIMIS/Corona water district evapotranspiration section is extremely specific to a single California water district — this level of detail is mismatched for a national audience and reads as AI-slop (exact quote: 'The ET data that Corona is using for the tiered rates comes from a CIMIS... weather station data located at UC Riverside'); (3) The '2026 Shift: What's Changing for Homeowners' section makes broad claims about 'many utilities moving away from legacy pricing models' without citing which utilities or jurisdictions — overgeneralized; (4) The 'Practical Calculation Example' ($4/$6/$10 per 1,000 gal tiers) is generic and not sourced to any actual utility rate card; (5) Duplicate internal links: links to '02-average-utility-costs-2026' appear twice in same section; (6) The 'Hidden Fees and Additional Charges' section correctly notes sewer and storm fees but does not quantify them — another missed opportunity for specific examples. FACTS: 'Tier 1 covers essential indoor needs (drinking, bathing, toilets, laundry)' — CONFIRMED (standard utility practice, verified via multiple water utility rate cards); 'Tiered rates create a strong financial incentive to conserve' — CONFIRMED; 'Tiered rates ensure high users pay proportionally more' — CONFIRMED; 'Cherry Creek Valley and Little Thompson districts announced tiered rate plans for CY 2026' — NEEDS HUMAN REVIEW — no specific source cited; 'Colorado HB 1090 effective Jan 1, 2026' — NEEDS HUMAN REVIEW — unable to confirm via web search 2026-08-29; '1 CCF = 748 gallons' — CONFIRMED (standard US conversion). WEAKCOPY: 'This billing system encourages community members to conserve water resources and use water more efficiently.' — filler, no information content. FIXES: (1) Remove or heavily reduce the Corona/CIMIS section — it's too specific and sourced to a single California district while the page targets a national audience; (2) Verify and either source or remove the Colorado HB 1090 claim; (3) Remove or generalize the '2026 Shift' section — cite specific utility examples or remove; (4) Add a real utility rate card example (e.g., 'Seattle Water's actual 2024 tiered rates are...'); (5) Condense the FAQ — 7 FAQ questions is excessive and several are same-content; (6) Add a cross-link to 'why is my water bill higher in summer' for seasonal tier impact. EFFORT: L · IMPACT: M — page is long but has unsourced specifics that damage credibility. SEO: 'tiered water rates explained' keyword; add 'water rate tiers' to tags.

CLUSTER OVERLAP ANALYSIS: The seasonal-water cluster (winter, summer, tiered-rates) has significant overlap with restructured pages (06-water-bill-too-high, why-did-my-water-bill-suddenly-increase). The winter page (846 words) overlaps with 06-water-bill-too-high (1,986 words, cause #5 billing period, #6 seasonal changes). The summer page (1,280 words) overlaps with why-did-my-water-bill-suddenly-increase (1,941 words, section on seasonal/irrigation changes). The tiered-rates page (3,092 words) overlaps with 06's cause #3 (rate/tier/billing change). RECOMMEND: Consolidate seasonal pages into a single canonical 'seasonal water usage' page, with winter and summer as redirects. Tiered-rate page should be the canonical for that topic (retain). 06-water-bill-too-high is now the canonical diagnostic page — the seasonal pages should defer to it rather than duplicate its content.

INSTANT-EXIT ANALYSIS: Tier-rank 14 (20-proration) has 77.8% BR with 1s TOP — the page is short and the user sees it doesn't deliver on 'explained' → instant exit. Tier-rank 13 (winter) has 55.6% BR with 28s TOP — moderate engagement but still below target. Tier-rank 16 (tiered-water-rates) has 33.3% BR with 44s TOP — the best performer in this group, likely because the content matches the user intent. Tier-rank 15 (summer) has 75% BR with 46s TOP — surprisingly high BR given the decent content. Since the summer and winter pages are similar in structure, the difference (55.6% vs 75% BR) may be season-dependent (winter = recent relevance, summer = not yet season).

E-E-A-T: All four pages have 0 outbound links to authoritative sources beyond EPA and ConEd. Tiered-water-rates has no government/utility sources at all — this is the site's #1 credibility risk. The EPA sources are present on winter (2 sources) and summer (0 sources — no sources section at all!). Proration (2 ConEd sources). Tiered-rates (0 sources).
